title: Can four pieces of a square make a bigger square with a hole?
description: Two perpendicular lines through the centre cut a square into four pieces that fit exactly on each other. The pieces are turned and slid out so that they form a larger square around a square hole. The pieces keep their area, so the larger square take away the hole is the original square.
teaching_notes: One idea: cutting and rearranging pieces does not change their total area. Watch for children who think a bigger square must have more material, or who forget the hole.

source: Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 6)
video_script.why: The child sees that congruent pieces cut from a square can be moved without changing their area, so a larger square with a hole has the same area as the original square once the hole is taken away.
video_script.substitution: Cut the square into four congruent pieces, move the pieces into the corners of a larger square, and compare areas.
video_script.anchor: the square that the book cuts into four parts with two perpendicular lines
video_script.payoff_line: the four congruent pieces form a larger square around a square hole

final_answer.value: The 4 congruent pieces form a larger square around a square hole; total area is unchanged
final_answer.spoken: the four congruent pieces form a larger square around a square hole, and the area is unchanged

hold_back: the 4 congruent pieces form a larger square around a square hole

maths_rules: two perpendicular lines through the centre of the square, not parallel to its sides, cut it into 4 pieces
a quarter turn about the centre sends the square onto itself, so the 4 pieces are congruent
each piece has a right angle at the centre and a right angle at a corner of the square, and two equal edges meet at the centre
the pieces are turned a little and slid out so the centre right angles sit at the 4 corners of a larger square, the two equal edges along its outside
the gap in the middle is a square because the 4 pieces are placed by quarter turns
area of larger square − area of hole = sum of the 4 pieces = area of the original square
video_script.design: One idea: moving congruent pieces keeps their total area. The cut square is shown first, then the pieces move out into the larger square with its hole. No lengths are drawn, because the book gives none.
open_questions: The book figure is not in the extracted text. The video assumes the two perpendicular lines meet at the centre of the square and are not parallel to its sides, as needed for four congruent pieces; the worklist says each right angle points outward and the long edges run round the outside, but the equal edges that met at the centre are the ones that lie along the outside.
